title: Frailty
full_review:
A deranged father enlists the help of his two young sons in destroying demons in the twisted tale "Frailty" (Lions Gate).

"Frailty" is the type of old-fashioned scary movie that creeps over the audience, slowly drawing them in before pouncing. However, its impact lessens the longer the viewer has been out of the theater. Directed by Bill Paxton, the film falters with narrative holes that require the audience to fill in the blanks and a few all-to-convenient details that become harder to believe once some thought has been given to them. Nonetheless, it is a ghastly, unsettling ride up until its jumbled, surprise ending.

As the opening credits role, a montage of Texas newspaper clippings announce a series of grisly murders attributed to a killer who calls himself "God's Hands." The film then cuts to a distressed man (Matthew McConaughey) sitting in the office of FBI agent Wesley Doyle (Powers Boothe), who heads the search for the notorious murderer. Introducing himself as Fenton Meiks, the man announces that the murderer behind the God's Hands killings is his brother Adam, who has just committed suicide. But Adam's crimes are part of a ghoulish family history Fenton must reveal to Agent Doyle in order for him to understand what motivated his brother to kill.

This sets in motion the first of two lengthy flashbacks where Fenton turns the clock back to 1979 and describes his bizarre childhood. The Meiks brothers, 12-year-old Fenton (Matthew O'Leary) and 9-year-old Adam (Jeremy Sumpter), live with their loving, sensitive father (Paxton), who is still recovering from the death of his beloved wife. The boys are happy though, with Fenton taking on the role of wife and cooking dinner each night as the brothers wait for Dad to come home. Then suddenly one night, their father wakes them up to say he's had a vision. An angel visited him and revealed his purpose in life: to kill "demons" posing as ordinary men and women. The angel will provide them with a list of names and weapons for the task. From then on, the Meiks family mission is to destroy these demons.

While Adam is enthusiastic about the family's divine justice errand, young Fenton is wary, believing his father has gone insane. The beauty in Paxton's portrayal is that the father remains calm and even gentle throughout. There are no outbursts of anger, but instead a dogged determination to do God's will as he has interpreted it, which is far more frightening. Yet the underlying flaw with Paxton's character (and some of the other characters as well) is that little background or motivation is revealed. Audiences are left to wonder whether this man was a Christian at all, much less one fervent about his "faith."

However, as director, Paxton builds up considerable tension as the film continues a murder-thriller path. The violence is disturbing, especially since the camera focuses on the faces of the children as Dad's ax comes down to slay another demon. The pressure mounts as the friction between young Fenton and his father escalates, leading to some pretty gruesome twists.

McConaughey offers a subtle performance, often giving his character more depth than is actually written for him. The young actors playing the Meiks brothers acquit themselves well, especially O'Leary since the bulk of the action lies on his small shoulders. Both as an actor and director, Paxton's execution is on target, keeping the flashback-flashfoward story on course.

The story of a disturbed father and a family poisoned by the evil it supposedly rejects terrifies because it takes a good thing like faith and doing God's will, and warps it beyond recognition.

Because of intermittent violence including suicide and some rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
